title: Lie Groups Turn Symmetry Into Calculus
notes: Open the lecture by naming the central compression of the chapter. A Lie group is a manifold with algebraic operations, but the reason the chapter matters is that global symmetry becomes local calculus at the identity. Tell students that the deck will keep moving information toward the identity: translations move tangent vectors, the exponential creates curves, determinant and trace detect tangent constraints, and left-invariant vector fields turn the tangent space into a Lie algebra.

title: A Lie Group Has Smooth Algebra
notes: Give the definition slowly, because it is the doorway to everything else in the lecture. The group axioms are familiar, but the new condition is that the two algebraic operations are smooth as maps of manifolds. Multiplication is a map from the product manifold to the group, and inverse is a self map. This means that all later constructions can be differentiated, so the algebraic structure can produce tangent maps, vector fields, and eventually a bracket.

title: Translations Move Calculus To The Identity
notes: This slide should make left translation feel like the basic transport mechanism. Multiplying by a fixed group element is a diffeomorphism, so its differential carries tangent vectors from one point of the group to another. The displayed homomorphism identity is the first sign that these transports behave naturally under maps of Lie groups. Later, differentiating this kind of square is exactly how a group homomorphism produces a Lie algebra homomorphism.

title: Matrix Groups Are Open Sets Or Constraint Sets
notes: Use this slide to separate examples by how their manifold structure is found. General linear matrices form an open subset because nonzero determinant is an open condition. Special linear and orthogonal groups are constraint sets, so tangent spaces come from differentiating equations. The important subtlety is the target space of the constraint map. For orthogonal matrices, A transpose A is symmetric, and using that smaller target gives the correct dimension count.

title: Lie Subgroups Have Several Geometric Personalities
notes: Students often expect every subgroup of a Lie group to inherit a neat submanifold structure. This chapter asks them to be more precise. Some subgroups are embedded, some are only immersed images, and compact groups can contain dense one-parameter subgroups. The distinction matters because the same algebraic subset can have different topological behavior depending on the inclusion map and the topology we put on the subgroup.

title: A Dense Torus Line Warns Against Naive Subgroup Pictures
notes: Use the square model of the torus because it makes the warning visible. A rational slope line closes up after a period, but an irrational slope keeps returning to new bins. The local parameter t still gives a perfectly smooth one-dimensional Lie group model, yet the image is not a closed embedded circle in the torus. This example motivates why the closed subgroup theorem is powerful but cannot be casually applied to every subgroup.

title: Closed Subgroups Recover Embedded Geometry
notes: State the theorem as an organizing rule rather than a technical detour. Closedness converts an algebraic subgroup into an embedded smooth object, so the surrounding Lie group supplies the right local charts and tangent spaces. This is why matrix groups defined by equations are so useful: once closedness or a regular level set argument is available, the infinitesimal object can be found by differentiating the equations at the identity.

title: The Matrix Exponential Builds Curves Through The Identity
notes: The exponential is the bridge from a tangent matrix to a curve in the group. Read the power series as the definition that makes sense for matrices, and then emphasize the derivative identity. Since X commutes with its own exponential series, the derivative can be written on either side. At t equals zero the curve is at the identity and the velocity is X, which is why exponential curves are the main way to test candidate Lie algebra elements.

title: SO2 Exponential Is Rotation At Unit Speed
notes: This is the most concrete exponential example in the chapter. The generator J is skew-symmetric, and its exponential is the usual rotation matrix. The recorded residuals are deliberately small, so the computational artifact agrees with the theoretical claim that the curve remains orthogonal and determinant one. Use this example to reinforce the rule students will generalize: tangent constraints at the identity tell us which exponential curves remain in a matrix group.

title: Trace Controls Volume Under Exponentiation
notes: Treat trace as the infinitesimal volume counter. The determinant of the exponential is exponential of the trace, so trace zero should be read as infinitesimal volume preservation. The cyclic trace identity is one of the algebraic reasons these formulas behave well under conjugation and commutators. The numeric residual is not the proof, but it verifies that the chapter artifact is measuring the same determinant-trace identity used in the lecture.

title: The Determinant Differential At I Is Trace
notes: This slide is the tangent-space computation for special linear groups. Linearize the determinant level set at the identity: the derivative of determinant in the direction X is the trace of X. Therefore the tangent condition for det equals one is trace zero. The picture separates directions tangent to the level set from directions that immediately leave it. This is the first explicit example of a Lie algebra appearing as a linearized group constraint.

title: Tangent Constraints Define Classical Lie Algebras
notes: Now put the determinant and orthogonality computations side by side. For special linear matrices, differentiating det equals one gives trace zero. For orthogonal matrices, differentiating A transpose A equals I along a curve through I gives X transpose plus X equals zero. These are not arbitrary definitions. They are the linear constraints forced by the defining group equations, and they define the classical Lie algebras at the identity.

title: Left-Invariant Fields Are Global Copies Of One Vector
notes: This is where the tangent space at the identity becomes global. Choose one vector A in the identity tangent space, then push it forward by every left translation. The resulting vector field is left-invariant because translating the group translates the field values in the same way. Stress that this construction is reversible: a left-invariant field is completely determined by its value at the identity, so the space of such fields is naturally identified with T_eG.

title: The Bracket Lives On The Identity Tangent Space
notes: The ordinary vector-field bracket lives on vector fields, not directly on tangent vectors. The left-invariant construction lets us transfer it. Given A and B at the identity, extend them uniquely to left-invariant fields, take the vector-field bracket, and evaluate back at the identity. The theorem behind the definition is closure: the bracket of left-invariant fields is again left-invariant, so the result is again controlled by one vector at the identity.

title: For Matrix Groups The Bracket Is The Commutator
notes: For matrix groups, the abstract bracket becomes something students can compute directly: AB minus BA. The table records the bracket among the standard sl2 basis elements H, E, and F. Point out two structural facts in the checks. First, the commutator of trace-zero matrices is trace zero, so sl2 closes. Second, the Jacobi residual is zero, matching the Lie algebra identity. The table is a compact lab for noncommutativity.

title: Homomorphisms Differentiate To Lie Algebra Homomorphisms
notes: Return to the translation identity from the beginning of the lecture. A Lie group homomorphism respects multiplication, so it respects left translations. Differentiating that compatibility gives a pushforward map from T_eG to T_eH, and the left-invariant-field bracket is natural under this pushforward. The result is a Lie algebra homomorphism. Mention the adjoint representation as the important self-map example: conjugation by a group element differentiates to a bracket-preserving linear map.

title: Inspection Lab Trace-Zero Stays Perturb It Drifts
notes: This lab slide is meant for active inspection. The trace-zero row stays in special linear up to numerical roundoff. Perturbing the matrix so the trace is plus or minus 0.16 makes the exponential curve drift away from determinant one, even though det exp X equals exp trace X is still being satisfied. Ask students to explain this apparent tension. The resolution is that the determinant identity predicts the drift; it does not prevent it.

title: Recap From Smooth Groups To Algebra At The Identity
notes: Close by giving students the full circuit. Smooth group operations allow translations and homomorphisms to be differentiated. Matrix constraints turn group equations into tangent equations at the identity. Exponential curves test whether tangent matrices integrate back into the group. Left-invariant fields move from individual tangent vectors to vector fields and back, giving a bracket on T_eG. The main takeaway is that Lie theory lets us study continuous symmetry by doing linear algebra plus one noncommutative bracket at the identity.
